4. The Rule is opposed by respondent No. 1 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that by Gazette Notification dated 27-1-2004 vide Annexure E to the petition the Government by amending the import policy order put restriction on import of Steel Re-rollable Scraps by the commercial Importer and, as such, the import of such item by the commercial importer on and from that date was banned. The Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 has defined the term "import' which means 'bringing into Bangladesh, in that view of the matter on the date when the goods were brought into the territorial jurisdiction of Bangladesh the restriction imposed by SRC No. 17 dated 27-1-2004 was applicable, the Commissioner of Customs rightly refused to assess the consignment as being a restricted item to be imported by the Commercial Importer. The order of the Commissioner of Customs being appealable under section 193 of the Customs Act, the instant writ petition is not maintainable. The moment the ship carrying the goods enters into the territorial waters of Bangladesh it would be subject to the control of the Customs Authority and would also be subject to any restriction imposed by the Government in respect of import of any goods on that day and, as such, the question of acquiring vested right by the petitioner or giving retrospective effect to SRO No. 17 dated 27-1- 2004 does not arise at all. 

 5. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury, Mr Hasan Rajib Prodhan and Mr MA Hannan for the petitioner, submits that respondent No. 1 acted without jurisdiction in refusing to release the goods on the basis of the bill of entry submitted by the petitioner on 25-2-2004 on the ground that by Gazette Notification dated 27-1-2004 goods in question were declared prohibited item for the commercial importer. Mr Mahmudul Islam submits that in the instant case letter of credit was, opened on 17-11-2003, the goods were inspected by the PSI Agency on 9-12-2003, the CRF certificate was issued on 26-1-2004 and the bill of lading was issued on 29-12-1003, i.e. the process of import was completed, before the imposition of the bar by the SRO in. question, therefore, the petitioner acquired a vested right to get the goods released on the basis of the letter of credit opened by him on 17-11-2003. And his said right cannot be taken away on the plea that the bill of entry was submitted after the embargo on the import came into force, He lastly, submits that in the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 (Act XXXIX of 1950) there is no provision for giving retrospective effect to any SRO imposing a ban on the goods which were already on board the ship, therefore, the' impugned order is liable to be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. In support of his contention Mr Islam has referred the case of A Hannan, vs Collector of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and others reported in 40 DLR 273, the case of Collector of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and others vs A Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, the case of Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co Ltd vs Income Tax Commissioner, Delhi and another reported in AIR. 1927 (PC) 242, the case of KS Paripoornam vs State of Kerala reported & Land Customs, East Zene, Chittagong and others in AIR 1995 (SC) 1012, Collector of Central Excise vs Azizuddin Industries Ltd. reported in 23 DLR (SC) 73 and Md Shoib vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Dhaka and others reported in 27 DLR 315. 

 6. Mr MA Aziz Khair, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for respondent No 1, on the other hand, by referring to the definition of 'import' and export' as given in section 2 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 submits that since before the submission of the bill of entry the government put an embargo by a notification in exercise of the power given to it by the said' Act prohibiting the import of the goods in question for commercial purpose, it cannot be said that the goods arrived in Bangladesh before the submission of the bill of entry, therefore, the petitioner did not acquire any vested right to release the goods being assessed on the basis of the letter of credit and the bill of  entry. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the only course open to the petitioner was to approach the Controller of Imports and Exports under Article 18 of the Imports and Exports Policy Order 1997-2002. He further submits that since the petitioner did not approach the Controller of Imports and Exports for permission to release the goods it has got no cause of action to maintain the writ petition. He lastly, submits that under section 16 of the Customs Act, the Customs Authority had no jurisdiction to release the goods in view of the embargo on the: import of the goods by notification dated 27-1-2004, therefore, respondent No. 1 acted within his jurisdiction in refusing to release the goods. The learned Deputy Attorney-General in support of his contention, has referred the case of Government of Pakistan through Ministry of Finance and 3 others vs Monzoor Brothers reported in 1995 SC MR 516.

 10. Now we are to see as to whether strict narrow meaning of the word "Import" as defined in Act XXXIX of 1950 can be made applicable in the instant case, particularly when the bill of lading was issued on 29-12-2003 and the embargo to import the consignment came into operation on and from 27-1- 2004, and as to whether the petitioner acquired any vested: right in assessing and' releasing the goods by virtue of his letter of credit and bill of lading opened and issued respectively long before the embargo. Mr Mahmudul Islam strenuously argued that practical aspect of the shipment of the goods shall also have to be taken into account, in order to apply the strict meaning of the definition "Import' as given in section 2(c) of Act XXXIX of 1950. 

 14. We failed to lay our hands on any provision in the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950, to give retrospective effect to the subordinate legislation to take away a vested right accrued to an importer, therefore, we find substance in the submission of Mr Mahmudul Islam that the acquired right of the petitioner cannot be taken away by giving retrospective effect to SRO No. 17 dated 27-1-2004 by which embargo was put on the import in question. We find support of our view from the cases of A Hannan vs Collector of Customs; Customs House; Chittagong and others, Collector of Customs vs A Hannan, Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co Ltd vs Income Tax Commissioner, Delhi and another; Messrs Paripoornam vs State of Kerala and Collector of Central Excise and Land Customs East Zone, Chittagong and others vs Azizuddin Industries Ltd as referred to by Mr Islam and noted hereinbefore.
